prohibited_recommendations: Do not discharge from the ED with a diagnosis of substance intoxication or primary mania without pursuing a structural and cognitive workup, given the clear 18-month prodrome.
Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD, NICE NG97 advises against it, and it may worsen behaviour.
Do not start memantine: a randomised trial showed no benefit in FTD and NICE NG97 advises against it.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls in this population.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
required_recommendations: Apply the Rascovsky 2011 criteria from the wife's history: state the features present (disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, stereotyped behaviour, dietary change, executive-predominant profile), the functional decline (dismissal, financial losses), and the level of certainty (probable, given the frontal and anterior temporal atrophy).

Explain why mania, intoxication and delirium do not account for the syndrome: an insidious 18-month course without mood elevation or reduced need for sleep, a negative toxicology screen and undetectable alcohol, normal metabolic tests, and full alertness and orientation.
Do not discharge with a psychiatric or substance label: arrange admission or early cognitive neurology follow-up to complete the work-up and confirm the diagnosis.

Address safety and capacity: driving, finances (the casino transfer; safeguard accounts and discuss lasting power of attorney), and documentation of the neurological illness for the legal process after the arrest.
Arrange caregiver education and support for his wife, and a plan for behavioural symptoms that avoids cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD and not part of the standard behavioral dementia workup unless rapid progression raises concern for CJD or seizures are present.
ECG has no role in the workup of a behavioral dementia syndrome; reserved for cardiac symptoms or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to the diagnostic question of a neurodegenerative behavioral syndrome.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in the absence of syncope, palpitations, or arrhythmia.
DaTscan assesses presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; not indicated here because there is no parkinsonism, tremor, or features suggesting DLB or atypical parkinsonism.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.

differential.key_features: Raised by the ED team; against it: an insidious 18-month course, no mood elevation, grandiosity or reduced need for sleep, apathy and loss of empathy, executive and social-cognition deficits and frontotemporal atrophy (Ducharme 2020).
The stolen item was cognac; against it: negative toxicology screen, undetectable blood alcohol, no increase in drinking, and the behaviour long predates this incident.

Negative toxicology screen, undetectable blood alcohol and normal metabolic tests exclude intoxication and delirium; the course and phenotype argue against mania.

red_herrings.intended_effect: A near-normal MMSE may falsely reassure the ED clinician that there is no significant cognitive impairment, supporting a primary psychiatric or volitional behavioral interpretation.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Approximately 70% of bvFTD is sporadic with no identifiable family history; absence of family history is the norm rather than the exception and does not argue against bvFTD.

results.finding: Three of six core features within the first three years define possible bvFTD. Probable bvFTD requires functional decline and supportive imaging.
results.source: Rascovsky K et al. Brain 2011;134:2456-2477 (FTDC criteria for bvFTD)
Bang J, Spina S, Miller BL. Frontotemporal dementia. Lancet 2015;386:1672-1682

results.finding: New mid-life behavioural change with functional decline warrants a neurodegenerative work-up.
results.source: Ducharme S et al. Recommendations to distinguish bvFTD from psychiatric disorders. Brain 2020;143:1632-1650

behavioural variant frontotemporal demen.summary: Rascovsky and colleagues (2011) define possible behavioural variant FTD by three of six behavioural and cognitive features, probable bvFTD by added functional decline and frontal or anterior temporal involvement on structural or functional imaging, and definite bvFTD by histopathology or a pathogenic mutation. New behavioural change in mid-life with progressive functional decline should prompt a neurodegenerative work-up even in a person with a psychiatric history. Treatment is supportive: SSRIs or trazodone for behaviour, caregiver support and safety planning; cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are not recommended.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Required core: structured behavioural/cognitive assessment with informant, urine toxicology and blood alcohol, baseline labs, non-contrast CT then MRI, and validated neuropsychological testing. Optional: FDG-PET or perfusion SPECT, literature.
metadata.notes: Emergency-department FTD case: a 61-year-old man after a shoplifting arrest with an 18-month bvFTD history. Teaching: resist acute-psychiatric anchoring; a negative toxicology screen and normal metabolic tests exclude intoxication and delirium but do not explain the history; a near-normal MMSE does not exclude bvFTD; CT first in the ED, then MRI and neuropsychology before any psychiatric disposition.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. R is a 61-year-old Hispanic man with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia who is brought to the emergency department by police officers and his wife following an arrest for shoplifting a bottle of cognac at a local supermarket. He has no prior psychiatric history. He is fully cooperative, minimally distressed, and appears puzzled by the commotion, stating he simply forgot to pay. His wife, visibly distraught, insists this is the fourth or fifth such incident over 18 months and that her husband is 'not himself.' She is the primary historian.

Approximately 18 months ago, Mr. R — formerly a responsible warehouse supervisor known for precision and interpersonal warmth — began showing gradual but progressive behavioral changes that the family initially attributed to occupational stress. He became less emotionally engaged, rarely initiating conversations with his wife or adult children. He stopped cooking, a previously strong interest, without explanation. His colleagues at work noticed increasing impulsivity: he twice confronted coworkers with disproportionate anger over minor matters, and he was ultimately terminated for insubordination four months ago. His wife reports that he appeared relieved rather than distressed by the termination.

Over the same period, his dietary behavior has changed markedly: he craves sweet foods almost exclusively and has gained approximately 14 lbs. He watches the same two action films on a daily loop, refusing to change the routine, and arranges his shoes and wallet items in a fixed order every morning. He has made two significant financial errors of judgment — an unauthorized $6,000 wire to an online casino and an impulsive purchase of sports memorabilia — without apparent remorse or insight into the consequences. When his wife cried at her mother's funeral he laughed, and he no longer responds to emotional cues from his children or friends. He has made sexually inappropriate comments to a neighbor, and the family had quietly covered up earlier thefts from shops.

The family reported no fever, no headache or neck stiffness, no focal weakness or sensory loss, no tremor, no falls, no hallucinations, and no seizures. There is no history of heavy alcohol use, illicit drug use, or recent medication change. His wife emphatically denies any increase in his alcohol consumption prior to this event.

The ED team is considering primary psychiatric diagnoses (late-onset mania, substance intoxication) and potential delirium secondary to a metabolic cause, given the acute presentation. No cognitive or structural workup has yet been initiated.
